Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'this mind is this buddha' (即心即佛): the first 'this very' (即) identifies mind, and the second identifies buddha. The phrase is recorded as a saying, a question, a quoted case, and the first member of a recurring contrast with 'not mind, not buddha' (非心非佛). In the record of Huineng and Fahai, Fahai asks for an explanation of 'this mind is this buddha' (即心即佛願垂指喻); Huineng answers by pairing 'the preceding thought not arising is this mind' (前念不生即心) with 'the following thought not ceasing is this buddha' (後念不滅即佛), then 'forming every characteristic is this mind' (成一切相即心) with 'leaving every characteristic is this buddha' (離一切相即佛). In Mazu's recorded exchange, when asked why he says it, he answers, 'to stop a small child crying' (為止小兒啼); when asked what happens after the crying stops, he says, 'not mind, not buddha' (非心非佛). Damei Fachang is later quoted saying that Mazu told him 'this mind is this buddha' and that, whatever Mazu now says about 'not mind, not buddha,' he retains the former words. Later masters also ask 'How is it when this mind is this buddha?' (即心即佛時如何) and place the phrase beside 'not mind, not buddha' and 'not mind, not buddha, not a thing' (不是心不是佛不是物).
Senses.Note: The exact four-character form occurs 955 times in 241 allowlisted texts. Definition-form searches found three occurrences of 'as for this mind being this buddha' (即心即佛者), one of 'the so-called this mind is this buddha' (所謂即心即佛), three of 'it is called this mind is this buddha' (謂之即心即佛), and one of 'call it this mind is this buddha' (喚作即心即佛); these mostly label or repeat the saying rather than independently define its words. The Huineng-Fahai passage is the fullest literal explanation found. Do not collapse the phrase into its paired reversal: the corpus preserves the sequence and later comments on both forms.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'this very mind is Buddha.' The variant 'this very mind is itself Buddha' (即心即佛) is used interchangeably. The stock public frame is Damei asking Mazu, 'what is Buddha?' and Mazu answering, 'this very mind is Buddha' (如何是佛；即心是佛). Sikong Benjing pairs it with another formula: 'if you seek to become Buddha, this very mind is Buddha; if you wish to ask after the Way, no-mind is the Way' (若求作佛，即心是佛；若欲問道，無心是道). A monk tells Nanyang Huizhong that 'venerable teachers everywhere also say this very mind is Buddha' (諸方尊宿亦言即心是佛), documenting that the phrase is corpus-wide rather than one master's property. Huangbo places it beside 'seeking Buddha outward' (向外求佛). The record also preserves explicit responses to the phrase. Asked why he says it, Mazu answers, 'to stop a small child's crying' (為止小兒啼); asked what follows once the crying stops, he says, 'not mind, not Buddha' (非心非佛). Damei replies, 'let him say not mind, not Buddha; I only say this very mind is Buddha' (任他非心非佛，我只即心即佛). Nanquan quotes Mazu and says instead, 'not mind, not Buddha, not a thing' (不是心，不是佛，不是物). Another recurrent line calls saying the phrase 'temporarily mistaking the servant for the master' (權且認奴作郎). These are recorded explanations, refusals, extensions, and warnings surrounding one lexical statement. They do not create additional dictionary senses for the statement itself.
Senses.Note: Zen-scoped variant counts: 'this very mind is itself Buddha' (即心即佛), 955 hits in 241 texts; 'this very mind is Buddha' (即心是佛), 388 in 120; 'mind itself is Buddha' (心即是佛), 73 in 44; 'one's own mind is Buddha' (自心是佛), 86 in 46. Counterpart phrases include 'not mind, not Buddha' (非心非佛), 727 in 213, and 'no-mind is the Way' (無心是道), 94 in 34. The earlier master-specific second sense was removed: Mazu's withdrawal, Damei's refusal, Nanquan's extension, and the stock warning are stances toward the same phrase, not different referents.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the ordinary or constant mind (平常心). Mazu's address supplies the most detailed in-corpus definition. After saying that the Way does not need refining but must not be defiled, he says, “ordinary mind is the Way,” then answers “what is ordinary mind?” with “no contriving, no right-and-wrong, no grasping-or-rejecting, no annihilation-or-permanence, no ordinary-or-holy” (無造作、無是非、無取捨、無斷常、無凡聖). In the Nanquan and Zhaozhou dialogue, Nanquan again answers “what is the Way?” with “ordinary mind is the Way” (平常心是道); when Zhaozhou asks whether one can head toward it, Nanquan says that trying to head toward it is already off. Other masters answer the direct question “what is ordinary mind?” (如何是平常心) with named daily acts and things. Changsha says, “when you want to sleep, sleep; when you want to sit, sit,” then “hot, take the cool; cold, go to the fire.” Zhaozhou says, “foxes, wolves, and jackals are it.” Xianglin says, “at dawn, the morning greeting; in the evening, take care.” These answers differ, but the headword continues to denote ordinary mind. The larger sentence “ordinary mind is the Way” is a proposition about that headword, not a second lexical thing.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 309 hits in 120 texts. The sentence “ordinary mind is the Way” (平常心是道) occurs 181 times in 100 texts, and the question “what is ordinary mind?” (如何是平常心) occurs 30 times in 19. Later records also warn against taking the sentence “ordinary mind is the Way” as an ultimate rule; that criticism concerns the same ordinary mind and does not create another sense. Item-8 readjudication therefore merges the former sentence-target sense with the headword gloss. Related family entries for the Way (道), “mind itself is buddha” (即心是佛), and “without contriving” (無造作) remain compatible with this description.

Senses.Explanation: The graphs mean “level or ordinary” (平), “constant or everyday” (常), “mind” (心), “is” (是), and “the Way” (道): "ordinary mind is the Way." The slogan has two attested loci in the corpus. (1) Mazu (馬祖道一): in his (示眾) recorded in (傳燈玉英集) (B14n0082, under the head 江西大寂道一禪師) — (道不用修但莫污染) and (若欲直會其道平常心是道) — with an in-text (謂)X gloss: (謂平常心無造作無是非無取捨無斷常無凡無聖), continuing (非凡夫行非賢聖行是菩薩行) and (只如今行住坐臥應機接物盡是道). (2) The Nanquan (南泉普願)–Zhaozhou (趙州從諗) dialogue: (趙州問南泉)。(如何是道)。(泉云)。(平常心是道) (so B25n0145; 無門關 case 19 平常是道 reads 南泉因趙州問。如何是道。泉云。平常心是道; also 景德傳燈錄 趙州章; 古尊宿語錄), continued (州云)。(還可趣向否)。(泉云)。(擬向即乖) (無門關; the form 還可趣向也無 is also attested, 15 allowlist hits) — and (道不屬知)。(不屬不知) (無門關) / (知是妄覺不知是無記) (景德傳燈錄). (天目中峰明本) records "this saying circulated through the monasteries" (此話流布叢林) and (古今之下鮮有不墮於意識者)。(盡謂著衣喫飯動靜語默一一天真). (平常心是道) is the full slogan; the shorter (平常心) is a separate, nested entry. The texts give the phrase the (謂)…(無造作)、(無是非)、(無取捨)、(無斷常)、(無凡無聖) gloss and the (道不屬知)、(不屬不知) continuation, and no gloss beyond these; neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Attribution (describe-only): the Nanquan–Zhaozhou occurrences are a two-speaker dialogue (趙州問 / 南泉/泉云) → MasterName null per the raised/dialogue rule; Mazu's (示眾) sits under his own section head (江西大寂道一禪師) as single-speaker instruction → (馬祖道一). The phrase is deployed as (a) Mazu's instruction with a five-negation self-gloss, (b) Nanquan's answer to Zhaozhou (無門關 case 19), and (c) a widely raised saying for comment (古尊宿語錄; 天目中峰廣錄 notes 此話流布叢林). Nested: (平常心) (t_4ccf8aed47d3) is the shorter constituent — a genuine constituent relation, added to RelatedTerms.

Senses.Explanation: Foot (腳) plus heel (跟), deployed in Chan verdicts for one's footing or the place under one's heels. The locative “under the heel” or “right where one stands” (腳跟下) appears in the stock verdict “right under his heel, worth thirty blows” (腳跟下好與三十棒), in statements about something shining through past and present right under the assembly's heels, and in the compound “the affair under the heel” (腳跟下事, 60 occurrences). The records also set two stance expressions against each other. “Plant the heels firmly” (立定腳跟, 24) appears in the instruction that one who travels and resides in the world must first plant the heels firmly and not be stirred by the eight winds. “The heels do not touch the ground” (腳跟不點地, 21; variant 脚跟不點地, 40) is used as a verdict about footing rather than a report of anatomy. The combined locative counts are 672 for the headword spelling and 731 for the variant spelling.
Senses.Note: Primary Zen-loaded sense, with the graphic variant “heel” (脚跟). The headword spelling has 1,607 hits in 211 allowlisted texts. The locative and opposed stance expressions retain the heel image but denote footing; literal injured or painful heels belong to the anatomical sense.

Senses.Explanation: The anatomical heel as a body part. The records predicate bleeding and injury of it: “the heel bleeds” (腳跟流血) and “the heel was suddenly injured by an axe” (腳跟忽被斧頭傷). These are bodily events, unlike verdicts about where someone stands or whether the heels touch the ground.
Senses.Note: No special Zen deviation is asserted for this ordinary anatomical sense. Two independent records anchor bodily predicates and prevent their absorption into the footing sense. The superficially anatomical phrase “heel pain, give [him] a beating” (腳跟痛與一頓) was excluded because its grammar awards blows rather than securely reporting pain.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, beneath the heel. Chan interviews repeatedly turn this ordinary location back upon the person questioned. A reply can be appraised with 'right under your heels, thirty blows would be fitting'; a master can ask 'how deep is the water under your heels?', direct a questioner to 'recognize it right under your heels,' or answer a request for direct pointing with 'look clearly right under your heels.' The phrase also marks relative position in a public comparison: if the monk can distinguish the kinds of leakage, Dongshan is under his heels; if not, he is under Dongshan's heels. A stock question asks about 'the matter under your heels' and receives 'putting a head atop your head.' The Chan-specific bend is consistent and observable: the spatial phrase becomes the immediate locus of an interviewer's demand, appraisal, or reversal, often contrasted with what the questioner seeks elsewhere or above. The texts do not supply a further object hidden beneath the feet, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: Zen-allowlist count: 672 hits in 176 texts. Deployment inventory includes blow-verdict, direct instruction, question, spatial reversal, and the compound 'the matter under your heels' (腳跟下事). Family check with heel (腳跟), underfoot (腳下), on the spot (立地), one's own part (本分), thirty blows (三十棒), and atop the head (頭上) supports one spatial referent used in several interview acts. Literal and loaded uses were not split because the loaded deployment keeps the same deictic location rather than naming a different thing.
